lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the state and its limits
lead.head: Bumping into the invisible state
body: Ajay Shah was in a spotless office, busy talking, when he turned abruptly to fetch his computer from a room. He walked straight into a glass wall wiped so clean that nothing showed it was there. {025-S01}
Amit Varma, after a joke at his friend’s expense, saw a metaphor. The state, he said, is “like that invisible fist”: we don’t see it, and it gets in our way when we least expect it.
Shah agreed. “The state is omnipresent, it invisibly reshapes our life and once in a while it slams into your face.”
The episode set out to make that wall visible: why the state exists, what it costs, and how far it should reach.
## The price of rights

Varma began with rights. They mean something only when they are defended, and defending them needs a state with a monopoly on violence. So we give up some rights to protect the rest, a paradox at the heart of liberalism.

His claim went further than saying that some state actions are violent. “I mean the existence of the state itself is at its core violence,” he said. Nobody would pay taxes unless forced to, and the state threatens to imprison those who don’t.

Taxes, direct and indirect, may take a third of your income. “Between January and April every year, you don’t work for yourself, you work for the state,” Varma said. We are all, in his phrase, in “part time slavery”. {025-C05}

None of this makes the state illegitimate, he stressed: we need it. But every ideology, communist, libertarian or social democrat, must answer the same question. When is this violence justified, and why? {025-C04}
## Scope versus strength

The second frame came from Francis Fukuyama’s *State Building*. Instead of arguing over big states and small ones, Varma said, ask how many things a state tries to do, and how well it does them. {025-C10}

On Fukuyama’s map, Sierra Leone does little and does it badly; the Soviet Union did everything, with middling strength. Varma wants limited scope and massive strength. India, he argued, is the reverse: it meddles in bedrooms and businesses and fails at its core jobs.

Shah rejected the middle-class idea of a strong state as one that can jail the powerful or pass a law overnight. Strength should mean competence: a polio campaign that reaches every child within a year or two.
Liberal democracy, he said, is meant to be slow. Power is dispersed and many people can veto, and that slowness is the design, not a failure of it.
## The tortoise’s pace

The same patience applies to growth. Many hope that 7 per cent per capita growth would bring India within spitting distance of America in 30 years. Shah said such growth, sustained that long, has essentially never happened.
“That’s a bad dream, that’s a wrong objective to pursue,” he said. {025-C14}

Asked once whether India should be a tiger or an elephant, Shah chose the tortoise, chipping away at sustained growth. The boom after 1991, Varma said, came from freeing parts of the economy so that people could discover positive-sum trades, not from growth targets.
Varma tied Shah’s phrase, “discover, not design”, to Adam Ferguson’s idea of progress through “human action, but not human design”.
Shah, signing off, counted the animals the episode had produced: a cat, a dog, a pig, a tiger, an elephant, a tortoise and a hare.

second.label: Law and certainty
second.head: Easy come, easy repeal
second.deck: Ajay Shah heard a boast about decisiveness as a warning about certainty
body: Ajay Shah was once discussing securities law with a policymaker in the UAE. The official waved his fist and made an offer: give him the correct securities law tomorrow, and he would have it enacted by the day after. {025-S06}
Shah drew the opposite lesson. “In my mind, I thought that there is then no certainty at all,” he said. A law that can be passed overnight can be changed overnight, leaving “complete legal risk”.

If there is any frictionless path for a strong state to push out new legislation, Shah argued, the legislation means nothing. {#frictionless} A healthy society has checks and balances, with many people involved in every decision and no strongman able to bulldoze through.

quote.text: Because if a law can be enacted tomorrow, it can be reenacted the day after.

second.caption: the law enacted by the day after

third.head: Rote players, rare masters
body: In his years as a professional poker player, Amit Varma saw many pros start out in a “stable”. A successful player, who could only play so many hands himself, would stake a group of players and coach them. {025-S02}

The coaching was mechanics: with twenty big blinds, here is your reshove range. Players memorised it and played correctly, “but they’re not thinking from first principles and figuring out shit themselves,” Varma said.
Only a very small share of the winners worked things out. Varma was always asking why.

Ajay Shah offered an engineer’s version: a technician trained on one air conditioner can repair it, but without thermodynamics cannot reinvent it. Hence his praise for the liberal arts, in some ways “the most useless thing in the world”, and the best kind of education. {025-C01}
third.caption: the poker stable

p2.title: The state of the state
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah, from first principles, on why the state exists and how far it should reach

sections.label: The method
sections.head: Ask why, then ask again
sections.caption: mechanics and first principles
body: Ajay Shah opened with a tension. He had recently written about public policy in the airline industry, a deep dive into one example. {#airline} Is it better to go one practical case at a time, he asked, or to learn general principles in their own right?

Amit Varma saw two tensions. The first is between mechanics and principles: his poker colleagues memorised what to play, while he kept asking why. Asking why all the time, he conceded, is a bit cumbersome.

The second is about explaining. A story grabs attention, but the principle it carries is often “adrift in space” and easily forgotten. A framework of first principles and root causes can be applied to everything, and its flaws are easy to find and discuss. {025-C02}
## Economics in everything
That is why Varma loves economics, which some call the dismal science. For him it is the study of human behaviour, and he finds scarcity and incentives in the best of literature, art and music.

Shah took it to education. Someone trained on one air conditioner can repair it; without thermodynamics, he will not be ready for the next wave of heat pumps. India, Shah said, valorises job-ready vocational education too much. {025-C01}
~ Both hosts value the humanities, Varma added, but universities provide them badly, so we must educate ourselves through books, movies and art.

quote.text: In some ways the most useless thing in the world is the liberal arts education. You’re absolutely not job ready.

sections.label: Framework one
sections.head: The mafia with a monopoly
sections.caption: the state as violence
body: Rights, Amit Varma said, have meaning only when they are defended. That needs a state with a monopoly on violence, so we give up some of our rights for the state to exist: the great liberal paradox. {025-C03}

We have normalised the state so much, he argued, that we forget its existence is itself an act of violence. Nobody would pay taxes unless forced. The state, he said, is like a monopoly mafia that holds you at ransom. {#mafia}
That does not make it illegitimate. Varma recommended Robert Nozick’s “great book”, *Anarchy, State, and Utopia*, but was clear: “I’m saying we need the state.”
## Who really pays
Nor is the cost borne only by the rich. The claim that only 3 per cent of Indians pay taxes, Varma said, is “absolute nonsense”. The beggar at the traffic signal pays tax when she buys tea. {025-C06}
Count direct and indirect taxes and a third of your income may go to the state, he said: from January to April we work for it, in “part time slavery”. {025-C05}
You want a space programme? “It is not money coming from the air,” Varma said. “Your domestic help is paying for it.”
~ Every ideology, he said, differs on one central question: when is this violence justified, and why? Acknowledge that, and “where you stand is kind of where you stand”. {025-C04}

quote.text: Whatever the state does, it does through violence. And therefore you have to justify that

sections.label: The other wing
sections.head: Rules without a budget
sections.caption: the two channels of state coercion
body: Ajay Shah offered a historical benchmark. The British taxes that kicked off Gandhiji’s Dandi March, he said, were “modest and decent” compared with the levels of taxation in independent India. {025-C07}
Then he split the state’s power into two channels. One compels people to pay money, which the government spends. The other tells them directly what they may not do, on pain of punishment.
The first channel has a check. Revenue is hard to raise, rupees are fungible, people hate paying, and the budget process brings some common sense. The second has no budget at all. {025-C08}
## Hundreds of agencies

“There is no single statement that details and documents all the acts of state coercion,” Shah said. Hundreds of agencies introduce one new coercion every day, and we have normalised the loss of freedom. {#agencies}

Amit Varma linked this to Subhashish Bhadra’s book *Caged Tiger*. America’s constitution, born of people fleeing persecution, protects the people from the state. India’s, written amid the violence of Partition, protects the state from the people. {025-C09}
~ The result, Varma said, is a mindset in which we exist for the state’s sake, to pay taxes and be subjects, and mission creep follows.

quote.text: Year after year, the state just layers on more and more and more coercion and nobody keeps track of it.

sections.label: Framework two
sections.head: Do less, but do it well
sections.caption: scope and strength
body: Amit Varma’s second framework came from Francis Fukuyama. Too often, he said, the debate is reduced to “big state bad, small state good”. {#bigstate}

Instead, think in two dimensions. Scope is everything the state attempts, from defence and law and order to temples, pilgrimage subsidies and space programmes. Strength, what economists call state capacity, is how well it does those things.
Sierra Leone is low on both and might as well not exist as a state. The Soviet Union had massive scope and middling strength. Varma’s ideal is limited scope and massive strength. {025-C10}
## Too much, too badly
India, he said, is the opposite. To set up a business in Delhi, he once read, you need more licences than to get a gun. {#gun}

The state interferes in everybody’s bedrooms and business and stops society from solving its own problems, yet fails at what it should do. Except for the privileged elite, Varma said, “there is no rule of law in India”. {#nolaw}
~ What the hosts want is the opposite: a state that does much less, but does it supremely well. Not a big state, Varma said, but a strong one.

quote.text: The ideal state, what I believe, is a state where the scope is limited and the strength is massive.

sections.label: The strong state
sections.head: Strong, as in capable
sections.caption: strength as competence
body: Ajay Shah worries about the Indian middle class’s admiration for a strong state. One version is a state that can grab the most powerful people in the country and put them in jail. {025-C11} The other is a leader who announces a new law overnight. Both, he said, are wrong.
Strength should mean competence: handling COVID vaccination so that as few people as possible die in a second wave, or reaching every child with polio vaccine within one or two years. {#polio}
Liberal democracy disperses power, with checks, balances and many vetoes. That makes it “appear slow and shambolic, and that’s a feature, not a bug,” Shah said. {025-C12}
## Ends and means
Amit Varma agreed that strong should mean robust. Rules should be framed so that even the most heinous strongman who comes to power can do only limited damage.
His heroes of the freedom struggle, Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar, Ranade and Gopal Krishna Gokhale, were liberal in their ends and conservative in their means. {025-C13}
~ Change, for them, came through engagement, discourse and dialogue. Hoping for someone to seize power and impose liberalism, Varma said, is not liberalism at all.

quote.text: If today somebody can come and impose liberalism, tomorrow somebody can come and lock you up and send you into gulags.

side.boxTitle: A slim book with a red cover
side.boxText: Francis Fukuyama’s *State Building* is a slim book, Amit Varma said, and everyone should read it. It swaps the big-state, small-state debate for two questions: how much a state does, and how well. {025-R11}

contQuote.text: So it is very important to see a healthy society as one where there are checks and balances, and then inevitably the state will be slow, will be deliberative, it will be consultative

stories.start: there was a very beautiful debate in the early years of American political thinking
stories.end: And I think we in India would benefit from thinking in these
stories.caption: America’s mad religious sects
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the strange origins of the secular state
stories.head: Mad sects and the secular state
body: In the early years of American political thinking, Ajay Shah said, there was a very beautiful debate. It begins with the people who built the country. {025-S05}

In Europe, Catholic and Protestant churches ran a regimented religion and persecuted people who wanted to do deviant things. Shah did not mean atheists. He meant sects crazier than mainline European religion would allow. Many of them fled and established themselves in America.
“So there’s a very deep idea in America that there should be freedom to pursue your own madness,” he said.

Nobody was thinking of a post-religious world. The sects were saying: don’t mess with me, let me be. Separation of church and state was meant to make room for them, not to open a path to secularisation and atheism, which is how the 20th century worked out.
That raised a question Americans took seriously. Suppose 20, 100 or 200 people decide to live in a commune with a boundary wall around it. Which of the state’s rules may they suspend? {#commune}
Some must hold everywhere, Shah said. The IPC prohibits murder, and you should not be able to create a commune within which murder is legitimate. {#murder}
In America, he said, you can create a new city or a new township, with your own rules to a significant extent. Shah called this a great source of energy for the American political project.
~ “I think we in India would benefit from thinking in these ways,” he said.
stories.why: The secular state began as a way of leaving religious oddballs alone. How far a community may set its own rules is a question, Shah argued, that India too should take seriously.

stories.end: paying thirty, forty bribes a month that it becomes incredibly uh hard to operate
stories.caption: the restaurant with one door
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a rule book nobody can obey
stories.head: One door, many doors, no way out
body: In an early episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, the restaurateur Madhu Menon walked Amit Varma through the plethora of licences a restaurant in Bangalore needed. {025-S04}
The excise department, wanting to see how much alcohol came in and went out, allowed only one door. The fire safety department required multiple doors.

No restaurant could obey both. “You’re breaking the law no matter what the hell you do,” Varma said. Restaurateurs anywhere in India, he added, are so busy paying thirty or forty bribes a month that it becomes incredibly hard to operate. {#bribes}
~ He called it one random example of a state whose scope is too vast: it interferes everywhere and stops society from solving its own problems.
stories.why: A state that tries to do too much writes rules that cannot all be obeyed, so every honest business becomes a lawbreaker by default, and the bribe becomes a running cost. {025-R12}

stories.start: I used to on my old blog India and Card I used to have
stories.end: regulating skirt hemlines, which is also sort of something that the state has done
stories.caption: where your taxes go
stories.kicker: Amit Varma reads from an old list of state spending
stories.head: Sixty-two elephants and a bill
body: On his old blog, *India Uncut*, Amit Varma kept a section called *Where Your Taxes Go*. It ran past number eighty and, in his words, “just kind of went on forever”. {#eighty}

He read out some entries. Moustache allowances. Educating and rehabilitating monkeys. Overpaying for condoms. Policing parrots. Salaries for fake municipal employees who don’t exist. Golf buggies for the army.
Then statues, hundreds and thousands of them, for whoever you fancy. “Sixty-two sandstone elephants is what I see on my list,” Varma said, along with the regulation of skirt hemlines. {025-S03}
~ The point was not only waste. Every item, he argued, was paid for with money the state takes by force, including from the poorest of the poor.
stories.why: An absurd line item is a moral question as well as a waste: each one is paid for with money collected under coercion, and that cost falls on the poorest too.

stories.start: I made this up Uh when I was at the Orange City Literature Festival
stories.end: where they chug away for a hundred years at modest growth rates
stories.caption: the tiger, the elephant and the tortoise
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s answer at a literature festival
stories.head: Not a tiger, not an elephant
body: At the Orange City Literature Festival, someone in the audience asked Ajay Shah about his dream for India. Should it be a tiger or an elephant? {025-S07}
“I want us to be the tortoise,” Shah answered: chip away for long years and get sustained growth. “The magic is sustained growth.”

India, he said, has instead had 20 years of high growth, from 1991 to 2011, and done badly thereafter. {#hare} The UK and the United States chugged away for a hundred years at modest growth rates, with decency, consultation and fewer mistakes.

~ Amit Varma at last understood Shah’s talk of a thirty-year sprint. Tortoises can live two or three hundred years, the hosts reckoned. “So for them, thirty year sprint kind of makes sense,” Varma said. {#sprint}
stories.why: Decency, consultation and fewer mistakes, kept up over decades, beat a heroic sprint, in Shah’s view. He said 7 per cent per capita growth for thirty years has essentially never happened in world history. {#never}
stories.postscript: Shah suggested the tortoise listens to *The Seen and the Unseen*. Varma said hares hear it at double speed. {025-J04}

quiz.q: What happened when Ajay Shah turned abruptly towards a room to fetch his computer?
quiz.a: He walked into a spotless glass wall and hurt himself a little.

quiz.q: Why, by Amit Varma’s reckoning, are we all in “part time slavery”?
quiz.a: A third of income goes in taxes: January to April, we work for the state.

quiz.q: Which two state departments set a Bangalore restaurant an impossible test, and how?
quiz.a: Excise allowed only one door; fire safety demanded multiple doors.

quiz.q: What are the two dimensions of Francis Fukuyama’s framework for judging a state?
quiz.a: Scope, how much it tries to do, and strength, how well it does it.

quiz.q: Asked if India should be a tiger or an elephant, what did Ajay Shah choose?
quiz.a: The tortoise, chipping away for long years at sustained growth.

quiz.q: Why does Shah think state coercion is a bigger problem than state spending?
quiz.a: Spending faces a budget constraint; nobody keeps a ledger of coercion, so it keeps growing.
